Computed-goto interpreter 9–13% slower when built with Clang 19 or Xcode 16.3–16.4: dispatch jumps are merged

When CPython is built with Clang 19, or with Apple clang from Xcode 16.3 or 16.4, the computed-goto interpreter ends up with a single shared indirect jump instead of one dispatch jump per opcode. Per-opcode branch prediction is the point of computed gotos; restoring it makes pyperformance 8–9% faster on Linux and 11% faster on macOS arm64 with Xcode 16.4. Put the other way round, current builds with these compilers are 9–13% slower.

LLVM 19 limited tail duplication of blocks that end in an indirect branch (llvm/llvm-project#78582). Clang lowers all computed gotos to one shared `indirectbr` block and relies on tail duplication to copy it back into each predecessor; the new limit stops that. LLVM 20.1.0 fixed this partially (llvm/llvm-project#116072) and 20.1.1 fully (llvm/llvm-project#114990). No 19.x release has the fix. Xcode 26.0–26.3 has the partial fix; it still merges most dispatch jumps, but the cost is only 1.4%.

GCC builds and the tail-calling interpreter (`--with-tail-call-interp`) are not affected.

Nelson Elhage [found in March 2025](https://blog.nelhage.com/post/cpython-tail-call/) that this LLVM 19 regression accounted for most of the originally reported speedup of the 3.14 tail-calling interpreter. His issue about merged dispatch jumps, gh-129987, was closed after gh-132295 and gh-132530, which changed GCC's SLP vectorization; Clang 19 builds still have one dispatch jump.

Use after free in getpath_isxfile() on Windows

`getpath_isxfile()` in `Modules/getpath.c` frees the path buffer before the last use:

```c
    DWORD attr = GetFileAttributesW(path);
    PyMem_Free(path);
    isxfile = (attr != INVALID_FILE_ATTRIBUTES) &&
              !(attr & FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY) &&
              (cchPath >= 4) &&
              (CompareStringOrdinal(path + cchPath - 4, -1, L".exe", -1, 1 /* ignore case */) == CSTR_EQUAL);
```

`CompareStringOrdinal()` reads `path + cchPath - 4` after `PyMem_Free(path)`, so the result of the `.exe` check depends on freed memory. The function is called during interpreter startup, when looking for the executable.

Only the main branch is affected: the early free was introduced in GH-153230, before which the buffer was freed at the end of the block.

# Description

When a value is yielded from an async generator and consumed via `async for` (or `await agen.__anext__()`), `_PyAsyncGenASend_Send()` (used by `SEND_ASYNC_GEN` and as `am_send` of the asend object since GH-148963) does the following for every value:

1. `async_gen_asend_send()` calls `gen_send()`, gets the wrapped value and passes it to `async_gen_unwrap_value()`.
2. `async_gen_unwrap_value()` calls `_PyGen_SetStopIterationValue(value)`: it allocates a `StopIteration` instance (including its `args` tuple) and sets it as the current exception.
3. `_PyAsyncGenASend_Send()` immediately calls `_PyGen_FetchStopIterationValue()`: it checks the exception type, takes the exception, reads `.value` and deallocates the exception.

### Bug description:

`search()` (and so `findall()`, `finditer()`, `sub()`, `split()`) can miss a match that `match()` finds at the same
position. It happens when the pattern starts with a scoped type-flag group, `(?a:...)` or `(?u:...)`, whose flag differs
from the pattern's own:

```pycon
>>> import re
>>> p = re.compile(r'(?u:\w)', re.ASCII)
>>> p.match('é')
<re.Match object; span=(0, 1), match='é'>
>>> print(p.search('é'))
None
>>> re.findall(r'(?u:\w)', 'café', re.ASCII)
['c', 'a', 'f']
>>> re.match(r'(?a:\W)', 'ß')
<re.Match object; span=(0, 1), match='ß'>
>>> print(re.search(r'(?a:\W)', 'ß'))
None
>>> re.findall(r'(?a:\W)', 'Straße!')
['!']
>>> re.findall(r'(?a:\W)|x', 'Straße!')     # an alternative disables the prefilter, and the result changes
['ß', '!']
```

**Cause.** `_compile_info()` builds the "charset" prefilter that `SRE(search)` uses to skip start positions.
`_get_charset_prefix()` looks through leading groups and combines their flags (`Lib/re/_optimizer.py:331` on main at
a57d16507cccb69d3d76ae05b52f01627d0bc479). It returns only the charset, though, and `_compile_info()` compiles that
charset with the pattern's own flags (`:428`). A category escape inside the group (`\w`, `\W`, `\d`, `\D`, `\s`, `\S`)
therefore gets the pattern's character type in the prefilter and the group's type in the pattern body. `re.DEBUG` shows
the mismatch (3.14.5):

```
>>> re.compile(r'(?u:\w)', re.ASCII | re.DEBUG)
SUBPATTERN None 32 0

The test `test_decompress_unconsumed_tail_after_eof` (added in gh-158169 / #158177) fails on main:

```

AssertionError: b'0123456789' != b''
```

Reproducer:
```python
import zlib

source = b'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'
remainder = b'0123456789'
dco = zlib.decompressobj()
data = dco.decompress(zlib.compress(source) + remainder, 1)

```c
    self->zst.next_in += left_size;
```

This advances `next_in` past the leftover input. The following block then computes:

```c
    Py_ssize_t left_size = (Byte *)data->buf + data->len - self->zst.next_in;
```

Since `next_in` was already advanced, `left_size` is computed incorrectly, so `unconsumed_tail` is not cleared at end of stream.

# Bug report

### Bug description:

Extensions compiled against 3.11 or older headers implement `Py_DECREF` as an inline `--ob_refcnt`. That includes abi3 wheels built on 3.11, which are common. Since 3.12 the interpreter hands out references to immortal objects without incrementing their refcount, so each such reference the extension releases is a net decrement. 3.14 starts immortal objects at `3 << 30` and treats `(int32_t)ob_refcnt < 0` as immortal, which leaves a margin of 2**30 (see gh-125174).

That margin runs out in real long-running processes. Home Assistant on 3.14.6 crashes after hours to days because PyAV's `cp311-abi3` wheels drain `True` by a few counts per `av.open()` and per FFmpeg log line (https://github.com/PyAV-Org/PyAV/issues/2420, https://github.com/home-assistant/core/issues/178218). A core dump from an affected instance had `_Py_TrueStruct.ob_refcnt == 0x7ffb2327`, which is 2**30 + 318,681 below `0xC0000000`.

- `PyStackRef_IsTrue`/`IsFalse`/`IsNone` compare the tagged bits exactly.
- `_PyStackRef_FromPyObjectNew` and `PyStackRef_MakeHeapSafe` decide whether to tag with `_Py_IsImmortal()`, which reads the refcount.
- `PyStackRef_FromPyObjectSteal` decides with `ob_flags`.

# Bug report

### Bug description:

Interrupting `loop.run_until_complete()` after its future is done means that the next run of the same loop can stop after one iteration. If the future of that run is not done by then, `loop.run_until_complete()` raises `RuntimeError: Event loop stopped before Future completed.`

```python
import asyncio
import signal

async def amain():
    asyncio.get_running_loop().call_soon(signal.raise_signal, signal.SIGINT)

loop = asyncio.new_event_loop()
try:
    loop.run_until_complete(amain())
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass
loop.run_until_complete(asyncio.sleep(0))
```

The above raises `RuntimeError`. The expected behaviour is that no error is raised.

If I understand correctly, this is due to the callback that stops the loop being missed by `remove_done_callback()` and thus deferred to the next iteration of the loop due to the timing of the signal.

Thus, this also affects `asyncio.run()` which runs the loop again during shutdown.

```python
import asyncio
import signal

async def amain():
    asyncio.create_task(asyncio.sleep(1))
    asyncio.get_running_loop().call_soon(signal.raise_signal, signal.SIGINT)

asyncio.run(amain())
```

This raises `RuntimeError`. The expected behaviour is that `KeyboardInterrupt` is raised.

# Bug report

### Bug description:

When a `ProcessPoolExecutor` worker dies abruptly, the executor manager thread runs `terminate_broken()`. That holds `_shutdown_lock` while it sends every remaining worker SIGTERM, sends SIGTERM again in `_join_executor_internals(broken=True)`, and then calls `p.join()` on each worker with no timeout. `submit()` takes `_shutdown_lock` first, as does `shutdown()` whatever `wait` is, and so does 3.14's `kill_workers()` (the repro calls it; `terminate_workers()` goes through the same `_force_shutdown()`). So if a remaining worker does not exit on SIGTERM, all of these calls block until it does, which can be never: once idle, the worker waits in `call_queue.get()` and never sees EOF there, because it holds a copy of the pipe's write end itself.

Workers outlive SIGTERM in ordinary programs. A SIGTERM handler that the main script installs at module level runs again in every spawn worker. coverage.py's `sigterm = true` handler can deadlock, or raise into the running task instead of ending the process (coveragepy/coveragepy#2310). # Bug report

```python
import sys

The script should print `�` (U+FFFD) on the console, since the UTF byte was not complete.

On new CPython versions, the `flush` call hangs, and this is causing an infinite loop.

I believe the problem was caused by https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/127325 Since that change, `WindowsConsoleIO.write()` removes an incomplete UTF-8 character from the end of the data on every write. list.sort() minrun computation is incorrect for very large lists on some architectures

### Bug report

`list.sort()`'s PowerSort implementation computes the mask used by the minrun generator as:

```c
ms->mr_mask = (1 << ms->mr_e) - 1;
```

Here, `mr_mask` and `mr_e` are `Py_ssize_t`, but the literal `1` has type `int`. For sufficiently large lists, `mr_e` can exceed the width for which this shift is valid/behaves as intended. On affected architectures, the shifted value becomes zero, so subtracting one causes `mr_mask` to become `-1`.

This breaks the intended PowerSort minrun calculation for very large lists and can cause substantially worse sorting performance than the intended O(n log n) behavior.

The issue was discovered while formally verifying CPython's PowerSort implementation in Lean as part of the ATLAS project:

https://github.com/facebookresearch/atlas-lean/pull/8

The formalization initially modeled the mask computation using the width of `Py_ssize_t`, which exposed the discrepancy with the C implementation: the C expression performs the shift starting from an `int`, even though the result is stored in a `Py_ssize_t`.

CPython's `Objects/listsort.txt` describes the intended computation as:

```python
mr_mask = (1 << mr_e) - 1
```

which does not have the fixed-width behavior of the C expression.

A minimal fix should be to perform the shift at the appropriate width, for example by making the left operand a `Py_ssize_t` before shifting.

Since gh-108518, the exception that `Executor.map()` re-raises for a failed call differs from 3.15 in two ways:

- `ProcessPoolExecutor.map()` no longer sets the worker-side traceback as its `__cause__`, so the traceback only shows `raise exc` in `_MapResultIterator.__next__`.

class E(Exception):
    pass

def f(x):

    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex:
        try:
            next(ex.map(f, [1]))
        except E as e:
            print('cause:', type(e.__cause__).__name__)
            ref = weakref.ref(e)
    print('freed:', ref() is None)

That seems reasonable to me, but I do not have the knowledge of the internals to say whether this is a bug, a known shortcoming, or by design, so I am reporting what was found and how to reproduce it. The analysis of the cause at the end is the agent's, and I cannot evaluate it myself.

## What the documentation says

The exception mode section of the `profiling.sampling` docs says samples are recorded when an exception is being propagated, "or when code is executing inside an `except` block where exception information is still present in the thread state". There is no mention of generators or coroutines being treated differently.

## What happens

An `except` block that runs inside a generator or a coroutine, or in an ordinary function called from one, is never sampled in exception mode. The same `except` block in a plain function is sampled as expected

`tomllib` reports an error position beyond EOF for some files ending in backslash

## Bug description

This is a fairly minor bug in `tomllib`: when a document ends with an unfinished backslash escape inside a double-quoted string or key, the exception reports that the error is *past* the end of the document.

```python
import tomllib

document = '"\\'  # A quote followed by a backslash.
try:
    tomllib.loads(document)
except tomllib.TOMLDecodeError as exc:
    print(len(exc.doc), exc.pos, exc.lineno, exc.colno)
    # 2 3 1 4
    # Doc length = 2
    # Error position = 3 (1 past the EOF)
    # Line number = 1 (correct)
    # Column number = 4 (1 past EOF)
```

The document has two characters, but `pos` is 3. I would expect the position to point either to the backslash or to EOF, which would be index 2 and column 3. As a practical matter the formatted message already says "at end of document", so this only affects callers using the location attributes.

The same thing happens for a trailing backslash in a basic string value or a multiline basic string. An unterminated string without the backslash, such as `'"abc'`, reports `pos == len(doc)` as expected.

The cause is [`parse_basic_str_escape`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/eb30e3d9d4b523e3f8de2cd1485c9ae9a996ab03/Lib/tomllib/_parser.py#L566-L594) advancing the position by two before checking the escape, even when only the backslash remains. ProcessPoolExecutor.shutdown(wait=True) deadlocks when worker exit messages fill the result pipe

### Bug report

`ProcessPoolExecutor.shutdown(wait=True)` can hang forever when the pool has many workers.

When shutting down, `_ExecutorManagerThread._join_executor_internals()` sends one `None` sentinel per worker and then calls `p.join()` on every worker. Each worker handles its sentinel by calling `result_queue.put(os.getpid())` in `_process_worker` before it exits. By then the manager thread has stopped reading `result_queue`, so nothing drains it while it waits in `join()`.
Once the result pipe is full, the next exiting worker blocks in `write()` while holding the queue's write lock. All remaining workers then block on that lock, and `join()` never returns.
Each exit message is about 21 bytes, so a default 64 KiB pipe only fills with roughly 3000 workers.
On Linux, however an unprivileged user who is over `fs.pipe-user-pages-soft` gets new pipes at the minimum size only 1/2 Pages. This is low enough to be high on high core count machines that run many processes.

I found this when running LLVM's `lit` test runner on a 512-thread machine. All tests finished, then `shutdown()` hung with 464 workers. At that point 389 workers had exited, one was blocked in `pipe_write`, and the rest were waiting on the queue's write lock.

Reproducer. `F_SETPIPE_SZ` is only used to simulate the small-pipe fallback deterministically:

```python
import concurrent.futures
import fcntl
import multiprocessing

F_SETPIPE_SZ = 1031

def init(barrier):
    global _barrier
    _barrier = barrier

Add an external flag to interpreter frames

### Feature or enhancement

I would like to add an `external` flag to the _PyInterpreterFrame struct. This would be a single bit, bit-packed into the same uint8_t that the currently unused `visited` flag is already occupying.

When anything besides the VM pushes a frame onto the frame stack (for example, anyone using the long-blessed PEP 523 evaluators or writing JITs), oftentimes there is metadata associated with those frames that needs correlation. In order to make that correlation, we need to know if a frame is associated with an external source. There are a couple of ways to solve this, but every solution that doesn't involve storing something on the frame itself involves maintaining a separate data structure and mutating it on every activation. This becomes especially difficult when dealing with arbitrary frames, for example from the perspective of either GC or a profiler/debugger.

The ideal solution involves having a bit on the interpreter frame that indicates it's safe to read some other data structure containing the metadata. For example, we could stack allocate the metadata immediately before the interpreter frame, and this bit proves it's safe to read.

This should have zero impact on memory, since it's using an existing bit. It should also have zero impact on performance until the point that the `visited` flag is actually used, at which point it should be negligible since it will be one additional mask.

## Link to the code that reproduces this issue

Minimal repro repo to follow; steps below reproduce it.

## To Reproduce

1. Create a page with `cacheLife("minutes")` (a prerendered shell with revalidate = 60s) and a server action invoked from a client component.
2. Run `next build && next start`. Wait over 60 seconds so the shell is stale.
3. POST the fetch action to that page repeatedly with header `next-action: <id>`, `content-type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8`, and body `["var_id",1]`.

## Current vs. Expected behavior

With `cacheComponents` on, a server action POST to a page whose prerendered shell is stale (`isStale === true` or `-1`) reaches the background-revalidation block in `dist/build/templates/app-page-runtime.js` (also `dist/esm/build/templates/app-page-runtime.js`, which Turbopack bundles): `scheduleOnNextTick` -> `responseCache.revalidate` -> `responseGenerator({ forceStaticRender: true })`. The condition for entering that block is `supportsRDCForNavigations && (isDynamicRSCRequest || isPossibleServerAction) && !forceStaticRender`.

That re-render uses the same `req`, so `handleAction` runs a second time on an already-consumed body. Actions fail with `SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input` (text bodies, e.g. `["var_id",1]`) or `Error: Unexpected end of form` (multipart). The log shows `MaxListenersExceededWarning: 11 end listeners added to [IncomingMessage]` first. A stack trace of the second `handleAction` call goes through `ResponseCache.handleRevalidate`.

Anything queued later goes onto `workStore.pendingRevalidatedTags` and nothing ever reads it again.

`dec2flt::decimal_seq` overflows an `i32` subtraction on a large valid decimal when overflow checks are enabled

When overflow checks are enabled, a valid 2,147,483,650-byte decimal panics in `parse_decimal_seq`:

```rust
d.decimal_point = s.len() as i32 - first.len() as i32;
```

The input is the 32-byte prefix `0.000000000001000000000000000080` followed by `2^31 - 30` zero bytes. At the subtraction, `s.len()` is zero and `first.len()` is `2^31`. The cast of the latter is `i32::MIN`, so `0 - i32::MIN` panics with checked arithmetic. The short control input, made from the same prefix plus 32 zeros, parses to bits `0x3d719799812dea11`.

Note: when overflow checks are not enabled, the overflow actually overflows to the correct value; there may no problem in that case.

The attached zip allows one to reproduce the problem.

I verified this in Rust 1.97.1, 1.98.1, 1.99.0, beta, and nightly source.

Lazy import lock contention (run in background threads)

### Bug report

### Description
When a lazily imported module is resolved (reified) in a background thread, the global import lock is held for the entire duration of that module's initialization. If the module has a slow initialization (e.g., heavy I/O, network requests, or computationally expensive top-level code), it completely blocks other threads from performing unrelated, otherwise fast imports.

This creates severe lock contention in multi-threaded applications that utilize lazy imports to improve startup time, as a background thread resolving a lazy import will stall the main thread (or other worker threads) if they attempt to import anything else.

Below is a minimal reproducible example demonstrating this behavior: 
```python
# slowmod.py
import time
print('-- [slowmod] Starting load...')
time.sleep(3)
print('-- [slowmod] Load complete!')
```

```python
# lazy_wrapper.py
lz = __lazy_import__('slowmod')
```

```python

shutil.move creates copy if rename fails with errors unrelated to EXDEV

### Bug report

(originally came across in https://gist.github.com/devdanzin/3198710e3c0128fda5e0a7b4e0768e5f 12/13)

If I `mv a/b somewhere/` with the permission of `a/` set to `500`/`r-x------`, I will get:
 ```text
mv: rename a/b to somewhere/b: Permission denied
``` 
and no `somewhere/b` is created. However if I use `shutil.move`:
```python
import shutil
shutil.move("a/b", "somewhere")
```

It raises with `PermissionError` which is also correct **but `somewhere/b` is created**. The correct behaviour should not create `somewhere/b`, as seen in the implementation of `mv`. If `a/b` is a very large file, the current behaviour of `shutil.move` will copy it first, which takes a long time, then raises with `PermissionError` and results in a duplicated copy of a very large file as `somewhere/b`, which is both bad to the file system and confusing to the user, also not matching what `mv` does.

The copy-then-remove fallback, after failure of `os.rename` captured by https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/shutil.py#L946,  should be performed only if the error from `os.rename` is EXDEV (failure because of cross filesystem), as suggested in its docstring and also [coreutils do_move](https://github.com/coreutils/coreutils/blob/master/src/mv.c#L168-L244). Other failure such as permission issue, disk error, file name too long etc., should not trigger the copy-then-remove fallback, but they are all currently captured by `OSError`.

### Bug report

### Bug description:

While an `imap()` or `imap_unordered()` iterator created with `buffersize` is waiting to be consumed, no other task submitted to the same pool is sent to the workers. If the program needs that other work before it reads more of the iterator, it deadlocks.

```python
import multiprocessing as mp

def sq(x):
    return x * x

def neg(x):

if __name__ == '__main__':
    with mp.Pool(2) as pool:
        a = pool.imap(sq, range(10), buffersize=4)

    pool.apply_async(sq, (7,)).get(timeout=5)   # raises TimeoutError

Doc/library/test.rst still says regrtest calls test_main()

### Documentation

`Doc/library/test.rst` describes how `python -m test` runs the regression suite. It says the runner imports each `test_*` module and executes `test_main()` when that function exists, otherwise loading tests with `unittest.TestLoader.loadTestsFromModule`. The same page tells readers to call `test.support.reap_children()` at the end of `test_main`.

That has not been true since `test_main` was removed as a regrtest entry point (https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/89392). `Lib/test/libregrtest/single.py` never calls `test_main()`. If the imported module defines it, the runner raises `Exception`. The module is then reported as failed with an uncaught exception (`test <name> crashed` on stderr, `failed (uncaught exception)` in the summary). Tests are always loaded with `loadTestsFromModule`. That collects `unittest.TestCase` classes and, when the module defines `load_tests`, runs the suite that function returns. Test packages add submodule tests through `load_tests`, usually via `test.support.load_package_tests`.

`reap_children()` is not called from `test_main`. Tests call it from `setUp()`, `tearDown()`, or `tearDownModule()` (for example `test_subprocess` and `test_pty`). The docstring of `test.support.reap_children` still says to call it at the end of `test_main()`.

The runner itself does not need to change. The documentation and the `reap_children` docstring should describe the current behavior.

Speed up pattern matching via shared checks

I've been playing with ways to speed up pattern matching. When several cases have the same shape, we often repeat checks and lookups that already succeeded. I think we can do better here. For example:

```python
match event:
    case {"type": "start", "value": value}: ...
    case {"type": "stop", "value": value}: ...
    case {"type": "pause", "value": value}: ...
    case {"type": "resume", "value": value}: ...
```

Here, every case checks that `event` is a mapping and looks up the same two keys. If the `type` value does not match, we do those checks and lookups again for the next case.

The idea is to find consecutive cases that start with the same work and share that part. Once we have checked the mapping and read the values, we can keep them and try the different `type` strings in order. If one does not match, we move on to the next comparison without repeating the common work.

The same idea applies to sequences with the same shape and class patterns that read the same attributes. We would still try cases in their original order and stop at the first match. We need to be careful with guards, since they can change what the next case sees.

This seems useful for longer matches where most cases only differ in a tag or a literal value. How much it helps would depend on which cases usually match and how much work they share.

### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

`PyMonitoring_FirePyStartEvent` results in incorrect duplicate calls to `sys.setprofile` profile functions

See https://github.com/bloomberg/memray/issues/1037 and https://github.com/cython/cython/issues/8032

The C API to programmatically trigger `sys.monitoring` events that was added in PR https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/116413 to solve issue https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/111997 and give Cython a way to trigger monitoring events for Cython frames does not work correctly with the `legacy_tracing.c` implementation of `sys.setprofile` profile functions.

When Cython uses `sys.monitoring` to signal that a Cython function has been entered, it creates a code object with `PyCode_NewEmpty`, sets a file name, function name, and line number for it, and then calls `PyMonitoring_FirePyStartEvent`. If there's a profile function that was installed by `sys.setprofile`, CPython's code in `legacy_tracing.c` registers an adapter callback that calls the `sys.setprofile` profile function. That adapter callback completely ignores the code object that is passed to it, and instead passes the `sys.setprofile` function the top frame of the Python stack, as returned by `PyEval_GetFrame`.

This interaction is completely broken: profilers installed by `sys.setprofile` never see the Cython frame, and instead see duplicates of the Python frame that called into Cython.

This could be fixed by CPython checking whether the code object that the monitoring callback receives is the code object held by the top frame of the Python stack, and refusing to call the `tstate->c_profilefunc` if not.

This is a tracking issue for the `movdir64b` and `movdiri` x86 target features (`#![feature(movdir64b_target_feature)]`, `#![feature(movdiri_target_feature)]`), used to gate the `_movdir64b`, `_directstoreu_u32` and `_directstoreu_u64` intrinsics.

`MOVDIR64B` (CPUID.(EAX=7,ECX=0):ECX[28]) moves 64 bytes from memory to a 64-byte aligned destination as a single direct store. `MOVDIRI` (CPUID.(EAX=7,ECX=0):ECX[27]) stores a 32- or 64-bit integer as a direct store. Both are on Intel Tiger Lake / Alder Lake and later, Sapphire Rapids and later Xeons, and AMD Zen 5, and neither is part of any psABI microarchitecture level. Today Rust code can only emit them with inline assembly, and `is_x86_feature_detected!` can't detect them.

- [x] Add the `movdir64b` and `movdiri` target features to the compiler and to `is_x86_feature_detected!` (rust-lang/rust#163742).
- [ ] Add the `_movdir64b`, `_directstoreu_u32` and `_directstoreu_u64` intrinsics in stdarch (rust-lang/stdarch#2239).

Vectorcall optimization can bypass a custom metaclass's __call__

### Bug report

The vectorcall optimization for class calls can skip a custom metaclass's `__call__`. This happens when a call site first specializes on a built-in class, then receives a class with a custom metaclass.

Reproduced with `msgspec==0.21.1`:

```python
import msgspec


class ValidatedAmount(msgspec.StructMeta):
    def __call__(cls, value):
        cents = int(value)
        if cents <= 0:
            raise ValueError("payment amount must be positive")
        return super().__call__(cents)


class PaymentAmount(msgspec.Struct, metaclass=ValidatedAmount):
    cents: int


converters = (int, int, PaymentAmount)
row = ("42", "2", "-100")
print([convert(value) for convert, value in zip(converters, row)])
```

Expected:

```text
ValueError: payment amount must be positive
```

Actual:

```text
[42, 2, PaymentAmount(cents='-100')]
```

The affected optimization is `CALL_BUILTIN_CLASS`. Its [runtime guard](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/333071231d3a46cccc32d7f44b99328c3299d0b1/Python/bytecodes.c#L4835) checks `PyType_Check(callable)` and a non-NULL `tp_vectorcall`. A class with a custom metaclass can pass these checks, after which the call handler invokes its `tp_vectorcall` directly, bypassing the metaclass's `__call__`.

Improve performance for list.insert() and del list[i] in free-threaded builds

### Feature or enhancement

`ins1()`(used by `list.insert()`) and `list_ass_item_lock_held()` shift the list with one atomic release store per element in free-threaded builds.  Those atomic stores prevent the compiler from vectorizing the loops, making them much slower than `memmove()` for large shifts.  I propose using the existing `ptr_wise_atomic_memmove()` helper here. It uses `memmove()` as a fast path when the list is owned by the current thread and is not shared, and keeps the atomic element-wise stores for lists that other threads can observe.

The default (GIL) build keeps the current loops because the compiler can optimize them directly in the calling function, and they perform better in benchmarks.

pyperf, free-threaded release build (--disable-gil, -O3):

    del l[0]                 2.26x faster
    del l[len(l)//2]         2.14x faster
    l.insert(0, x)           1.95x faster
    l.insert(len(l)//2, x)   1.86x faster
    insert(0)+del[0], n=1000 2.86x faster
    sliding window, n=1000   2.46x faster

Compiling both versions in GIL mode produces the same code for `ins1()` and `list_ass_item_lock_held()`, so the default build is not affected.

This continues gh-129069, which introduced `ptr_wise_atomic_memmove()`.

Segfault when a finalizer declares or resolves a lazy import during shutdown

### Crash report

**Bug:** If a finalizer declares or resolves a lazy import during shutdown, CPython can segfault.

This is a corner case where both of the following must exist:
- a lazy object whose `__import__` still works at shutdown;
- a holder that outlives the lazy-import state, such as a `ContextVar`, the codec registry, fork callbacks, audit hooks or warnings filters.

**Why:** Shutdown frees `lazy_modules` and `lazy_pending_submodules` and sets them to NULL, but finalizers can still run after they have been freed and we do not have the necessary NULL checks in place to handle reachable functions accessing either nulled object.

**Minimal repro:**

    return allowed[name]

ns = types.ModuleType("ns")
ns.json = __lazy_import__("json", {"__builtins__": {"__import__": safe_import}})

class Handle:
    def __del__(self, ns=ns):
        ns.json

contextvars.ContextVar("v").set(Handle())

`LogRecord` should normalize falsy `exc_info` values

### Bug report

Pointed out by @tjkuson in python/typeshed#16466

[According to the documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging.Logger.debug), the  `exc_info` argument to the `log()` group of function can be any falsy value to indicate that no exception information is provided. It's common to use either `None` or `False` here.

When a truthy value is provided, it is normalized to an exception info tuple before passing it to `LogRecord`. A falsy value is passed on unchanged:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/9112daed900c3314fa522043fc64ddbb2ecd4ca5/Lib/logging/__init__.py#L1678-L1682

This contradicts [LogRecords documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging.LogRecord), which says that only `None` is accepted and that the `exc_info` field can be a tuple or `None`. The mypy primer run in python/typeshed#16466 shows that a few projects make this assumption. For example, [sphinx](https://github.com/sphinx-doc/sphinx/blob/b04a2101295ac3fb725b16111eda0284b6da4cca/sphinx/util/logging.py#L410-L411):

```python
        if record.exc_info is not None:
            raise SphinxWarning(message) from record.exc_info[1]
```

Solution: Normalize falsy values to `None` before passing them to `makeRecord`.

pegen: leader selection for left-recursive SCCs takes factorial time

# Feature or enhancement

### Proposal:

When pegen picks a leader for a left-recursive SCC, `compute_left_recursives` calls `sccutils.find_cycles_in_scc` from every node. That function walks every path through the SCC, so the work grows factorially with the SCC's size.

CPython's own grammar doesn't notice, because its biggest left-recursive SCC has two rules. But a third-party grammar with a handful of mutually left-recursive rules makes generation fall over:

| mutually left-recursive rules | parser generation |
|---|---|
| 10 | 30 ms |
| 14 | 2.5 s |
| 9, with no valid leader (error path) | 0.48 s |

On a fully connected 8-rule SCC, that's about 1.07 million name comparisons before it reports "no leadership candidate".

A leader is a rule that sits on every cycle in the SCC. So you can test each candidate directly: remove it and check whether the rest is acyclic (a topological sort). That's O(V·(V+E)) per SCC, it picks the same leader (smallest name), and it raises the same error. The 14-rule case drops to about 8 ms, and the generated `Parser/parser.c` doesn't change.

I have a patch with tests ready.

Enum creation is quadratic in the number of members (`_hashable_values_` list scan)

# Bug report

### Bug description:

Creating an Enum is quadratic in the number of members again. When each member is added, `_proto_member.__set_name__` runs `value not in enum_class._hashable_values_`, and `_hashable_values_` is a list, so every new member scans all the ones before it.

```python
import time
from enum import Enum

for n in (1000, 4000, 8000, 16000):
    members = {f'M{i:08x}': i for i in range(n)}
    t = time.perf_counter()
    Enum('Generated', members)
    print(n, f'{(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3:.0f} ms')
```

On main (3.16 dev, macOS arm64): 5.8 / 54 / 187 / 713 ms. Each doubling of `n` costs about 4x.

This is the same symptom as gh-89580, which was fixed. The `_hashable_values_` scan came in later.

The scan is only needed when the value was already in `_value2member_map_` before this member was added, for example an alias or a Flag pseudo-member that the class cached earlier. If `setdefault` just added the key, the value can't be in the list yet.

tarfile stream writes get slower as copybufsize grows

# Bug report

### Bug description:

`tarfile._Stream.__write` writes one block and then does `self.buf = self.buf[self.bufsize:]`, so it copies the whole remaining buffer for every block. Each chunk passed in costs O(chunk² / bufsize). At the default `copybufsize` (16 KiB) that doesn't matter, but raise it and stream writes slow down a lot:

```python
import io, tarfile, time
data = b'x' * (64 << 20)
for c in (16 << 10, 1 << 20, 4 << 20):
    out = io.BytesIO(); t = time.perf_counter()
    with tarfile.open(fileobj=out, mode='w|', copybufsize=c) as tf:
        ti = tarfile.TarInfo('f'); ti.size = len(data)
        tf.addfile(ti, io.BytesIO(data))
    print(c >> 10, 'KiB', f'{(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3:.0f} ms')
```

On main (3.16 dev, macOS arm64), 64 MiB takes 14 ms at 16 KiB, 55 ms at 1 MiB, and 215 ms at 4 MiB. A bigger copy buffer should be faster, not slower.

Fix: write each whole block straight from `buf`, then keep only the remainder.

xml.dom.minidom: Node.normalize() is quadratic in the number of adjacent text nodes

`xml.dom.minidom.Node.normalize()` merges adjacent text nodes with `node.data = node.data + child.data`, once per absorbed node. A run of n text nodes copies the growing string n times, so it's quadratic.

```python
from xml.dom.minidom import Document
doc = Document()
root = doc.appendChild(doc.createElement('r'))
for _ in range(32_000):
    root.appendChild(doc.createTextNode('x' * 48))
root.normalize()  # ~450 ms; 8k nodes ~25 ms, 16k ~95 ms
```

The parsers already merge character data, so you only hit this with documents built through the DOM API (appendChild/createTextNode, etc.).

Fix: collect the pieces for each run and `''.join` them once at the end. I'll open a PR.

Improve performance of dict merges by avoiding incref/decref pairs

### Feature or enhancement

The per-item loop in `dict_dict_merge()` takes an extra reference to `key` and `value` before dispatching on `override`. On the `override == 1` path `insertdict()` already receives its own references through `Py_NewRef()` and
nothing uses `key` or `value` afterwards, so the outer pair is wasted refcount operations per item (atomic ones in the free-threaded build). The pair is still needed on the other path, where `_PyDict_Contains_KnownHash()` can run `__eq__` and `*dupkey` hands the reference to the caller.

`override == 1` covers `dict.update(d)`, `d1 \| d2`, `{**a, **b}`, any merge into an empty dict, and `dict(d)` / `d.copy()` when the key-table clone fast path does not apply (sparse, split-table or subclass source).

I expected to see this happen: the gcc_submodule tidy check should gracefully skip with a message like "Cannot figure out the SHA of the GCC submodule", as its own comment claims ("Git is not available or we are in a tarball").

The fix is to match on the Result of .output() and emit check.message(...) in the Err branch instead of .expect().

Optimize dict insertion and deletion by avoiding a second probe

### Feature or enhancement

### Proposal

Inserting a str key probes the dict index table twice: the lookup decides
whether the key is present, then `find_empty_slot()` walks the same probe
sequence to find the slot to insert into.  Deleting probes twice as well
(lookup + `lookdict_index()`).

I'd like the first probe to report the slot it ends on, so the
insert/delete path can reuse it:

* on a hit: the slot that refers to the entry (what `lookdict_index()`
  returns);
* on a miss: the slot `find_empty_slot()` would return (the first dummy
  in the GIL build, the empty slot in the free-threaded build).

### Scope

Only exact str keys in all-unicode tables can use it.  That comparison
(pointer equality, cached hash, `memcmp`) cannot execute Python code, therefore
the dict cannot be resized or mutated while the probe is running.  For
other keys `__eq__` can run arbitrary code and invalidate the slot, so
they keep today's two-probe behaviour.  Readers pass a NULL slot and
generate the same code as before.

### Numbers

Prototype, `Objects/dictobject.c` only.  Per-metric subprocesses, medians
of 11 runs. the dict code built with `-O3 -DNDEBUG`, otherwise a

I noticed the slowdown always appeared suddenly past a few tens of threads, so I started to investigate that.

On the free-threaded build, a lock that many threads take at the same time doesn't slow down gradually with the number of threads: past some point, it collapses. ### Bug report

I don't have an actual failure to report: it's a potential issue I noticed while inspecting the code.

An asyncio.Runner on the main thread installs a SIGINT handler using `signal.signal` (and NOT `loop.add_signal_handler` for whatever reason). The signal handler could thus run at more-or-less any time and cannot rely on the asyncio machinery being in a consistent state. However, it directly interacts with the main task, calling `main_task.done()` and `main_task.cancel()`:

```python

        self._interrupt_count += 1
        if self._interrupt_count == 1 and not main_task.done():
            main_task.cancel()
            # wakeup loop if it is blocked by select() with long timeout
            self._loop.call_soon_threadsafe(lambda: None)
            return
        raise KeyboardInterrupt()
```

# ProxyBasicAuthHandler may send HTTPS-scoped credentials to a direct HTTP origin after a 407 response

## Summary

When an application explicitly installs `ProxyBasicAuthHandler` with an `HTTPPasswordMgr` containing credentials scoped to `https://HOST/`, a direct (non-proxied) HTTP server at the same authority can return `407 Proxy Authentication Required` with the matching realm. `ProxyBasicAuthHandler.http_error_407()` looks up credentials using `req.host`, which is scheme-less. `HTTPPasswordMgr` intentionally allows a scheme-less lookup to match credentials stored for any scheme, so the handler retries the direct HTTP request with a `Proxy-Authorization: Basic ...` header. The direct origin receives the HTTPS-scoped password in cleartext.

This requires a non-default opener configuration (the application must register `ProxyBasicAuthHandler`), a credential entry for the same authority at the root path, and a direct HTTP request to that authority. With a regular `HTTPPasswordMgr`, the server must know/challenge the configured realm. This does not describe normal proxy authentication: in a genuine proxy request `req.host` is the proxy authority.

## Details

In `Lib/urllib/request.py`, `ProxyBasicAuthHandler.http_error_407()` passes `req.host` to `http_error_auth_reqed()`. For a direct HTTP request, that is the origin authority, without `http://`. Excessive stack use in _PyModule_IsPossiblyShadowing

### Bug report

While debugging a test failure of [ft_utils.tests.test_localwrapper.TestLocalWrapperAttributes.test_recursion_guard](https://github.com/facebookincubator/ft_utils/blob/eb3547b4a6a710205f79f1aacbb8659f24c45a39/ft_utils/tests/test_localwrapper.py#L877) I noticed `_PyModule_IsPossiblyShadowing` stack-allocating not one, but *two* `MAXPATHLEN`-sized `wchar_t` buffers. (The second buffer is only used when `sys.path[0]` is `""`, which should be pretty rare given that it's normalized very early on in Python's startup.) The two buffers push the function's stack size past 32k, which means a call to it while producing a `RecursionError` can cause a stack overrun.

I haven't been able to reproduce such a case because of other protections involved, but when `_PyModule_IsPossiblyShadowing` is inlined into `_Py_module_getattro` (via `_Py_module_getattro_imp`l), _any_ attribute lookup ends up using 32k+ stack and that is a much bigger deal. Arguably this is a case of bad inlining decisions, but since it's fairly trivial and equally arguably more efficient to heap allocate the buffers here (given that the second allocation is very unlikely to be necessary), I think we should fix `_PyModule_IsPossiblyShadowing`. I have a PR for this.

Specialisation fail `LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE` specialised when no instance variable

### Bug report

```python
def test_load_attr_class_default_not_set_on_instance(self):
    class C:
        timeout = 30

        def set_timeout(self, value):
            self.timeout = value  # puts "timeout" in C's shared keys

    c = C()  # never sets timeout, so c.timeout is the class default

    @reset_code
    def get_timeout(n):
        for _ in range(n):
            value = c.timeout
        return value

    self.assertEqual(get_timeout(_testinternalcapi.SPECIALIZATION_THRESHOLD), 30)
    # Must load the class attribute, not specialize as an instance
    # attribute load that misses on every execution.
    self.assert_specialized(get_timeout, "LOAD_ATTR_NONDESCRIPTOR_WITH_VALUES")
    self.assert_no_opcode(get_timeout, "LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE")

    # Setting the attribute on the instance must be seen.
    c.set_timeout(5)
    self.assertEqual(get_timeout(1), 5)
```

This is due to `instance_has_key` returning `True` even if setting an instance field is not actually set. Json dumps shows this issue with many instance level attributes not set by default relying on class level defaults https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/978a8befa5ec9b28b161a56b16d326330aef4733/Lib/json/encoder.py#L156

For json.dumps this can add about a 5% tax due to missed optimisations although it depends on the payload size. `threading.Condition` is another example from the stdlib.

Rework `Modules/getbuildinfo.c` to build strings at build time, instead of runtime

Python has a collection of C files to get "build information"

* Modules/getbuildinfo.c
* Python/getcompiler.c
* Python/getcopyright.c
* Python/getplatform.c
* Python/getversion.c

_Py_gitidentifier(), Py_GetBuildInfo() and Py_GetVersion() build strings at runtime. For example, Python/getversion.c uses a static buffer of a fixed size: `static char version[300];`. _pyio.BytesIO.readinto() advances the stream when passed a read-only buffer

### Bug description

The pure Python implementation of `BytesIO.readinto()` and `readinto1()` consumes input before rejecting a read-only destination buffer. The C implementation rejects the same argument without advancing the stream.

```python
import io
import _pyio

for module in (io, _pyio):
    stream = module.BytesIO(b"abcdef")
    try:
        stream.readinto(b"xxx")
    except TypeError:
        print(module.__name__, stream.tell(), stream.read())
```

Output on main:

```text
io 0 b'abcdef'
_pyio 3 b'def'
```

The same happens with `readinto1()` and with a read-only `memoryview`. The destination is invalid because `readinto()` requires a writable bytes-like object, but rejecting it should not consume the input first.

The cause is in `_pyio.BufferedIOBase._readinto()`: it calls `self.read()` or `self.read1()` before the assignment to the destination memoryview raises `TypeError`. `BytesIO` inherits this implementation. Checking the memoryview's `readonly` flag before reading avoids changing the stream state and matches the C implementation.

I have prepared a focused fix and a regression test shared by the C and pure Python BytesIO implementations. The test covers both methods, bytes and memoryview destinations, empty destinations, and positions at the beginning, near EOF, and beyond EOF. On the original implementation the C test passes and the Python test fails eight subcases because the stream position changes. Both pass with the fix, and the full `test_io` package

tar_filter behavior with links outside the destination is not clearly documented

### Bug report

The `tar` extraction filter allows archive members to create hard links or symbolic links that point outside the extraction directory.

I understand from the security response that this is intentional, mainly to allow things such as `/dev/null` and other system paths. However, I think the current documentation does not make the security implications of this behavior clear enough.

The documentation for `tar_filter` currently describes it as refusing to extract files whose absolute path, after following symlinks, would end up outside the destination. This can be easy to interpret as meaning that links themselves are restricted to the extraction directory.

For example, an archive can contain a hard link with an absolute target such as:

```text
/home/user/example
```

When extracted with:

```python
tar.extractall(destination, filter="tar")
```

the hard link can point to the existing file outside `destination`.

This is different from the behavior of the `data` filter, which rejects links that point outside the destination.

I think the `tar_filter` documentation should explicitly state that:

* Links are allowed to point outside the extraction directory.
* This includes both absolute and relative link targets where applicable.
* Extracting an untrusted archive with `filter="tar"` may therefore create links to files outside the extraction directory.
* Applications that need to safely extract untrusted archives should use the `data` filter instead.

Docs: -X disable_remote_debug is spelled with an underscore, but the interpreter only accepts disable-remote-debug

### Documentation

The `-X` option that disables remote debugging (PEP 768) is documented as
`-X disable_remote_debug` (underscore) in three places:

- `Doc/using/cmdline.rst` (the `-X` list and the `PYTHON_DISABLE_REMOTE_DEBUG` entry)
- `Doc/howto/remote_debugging.rst` (two places)

But the interpreter only recognises the hyphenated spelling:
`Python/initconfig.c` calls `config_get_xoption(config, L"disable-remote-debug")`,
and `python --help-xoptions` prints `-X disable-remote-debug`. `Doc/whatsnew/3.14.rst`
also uses the hyphen.

Unknown `-X` options are silently ignored, so anyone who copies the documented
spelling ends up with remote debugging still **enabled**, with no error.

```console
$ python3.14 -X disable_remote_debug -c "import sys; print(sys.is_remote_debug_enabled())"
True
$ python3.14 -X disable-remote-debug -c "import sys; print(sys.is_remote_debug_enabled())"
False
```

Same result on 3.15.0rc3. Because this option is a security control, the silent
no-op is the important part. Suggested fix: use `disable-remote-debug` in
`cmdline.rst` and `remote_debugging.rst`.

# Bug report

### Bug description:

The 3.13 backport of gh-152563 (#155753, commit 8e85d73bd6) changed the skip condition of `FMATests.test_fma_zero_result` in `Lib/test/test_math.py` to:

```python
or (support.linked_to_musl() and support.linked_to_musl() < (1, 2, 6)),  # gh-131032
```

On `main`/3.14, `support.linked_to_musl()` returns the musl version as a tuple. On the 3.13 branch it still returns a plain `bool` (`return ('musl' in stdout)`), so on a musl-based system the condition evaluates `True < (1, 2, 6)` and raises:

```
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'bool' and 'tuple'
```

Because this happens inside the `@unittest.skipIf(...)` decorator, it is raised at class definition time and `test_math` fails to import entirely. `test_cmath` imports from `test.test_math`, so it fails too. On glibc the expression short-circuits on `False`, so it doesn't show up there.

This is a regression in 3.13.16. A visible consequence: building 3.13.16 on Alpine Linux with `--enable-optimizations` fails, because both modules are part of the PGO training set:

```

[27/43] test_math failed (uncaught exception)
Total test files: run=43/43 failed=2
Result: FAILURE
make: *** [Makefile:911: profile-run-stamp] Error 2
```

To fix it, either restore the previous `or support.linked_to_musl(),` condition on 3.13, or also backport the `linked_to_musl()` change that returns a version tuple.

# Feature or enhancement

### Proposal:

The performance regression suite I run against CPython builds picked up a small slowdown in `tempfile` after #150477, which added the `ValueError` for a `prefix` or `suffix` with a directory component (gh-79459).

The check calls `os.path.dirname()` twice in `_sanitize_params()`, which runs on every `mkstemp()`, `mkdtemp()`, `NamedTemporaryFile()` and so on. A typical case is a function that processes a batch of uploaded documents and writes each one to a temporary file, because the library it hands them to only accepts a path:

```python
for document in batch:
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".pdf") as f:
        f.write(document)
        f.flush()
        extract_text(f.name)
```

On Lambda x86_64 (PGO+LTO), `_sanitize_params()` got about 56% slower, and creating 512 real files in `/tmp` about 2% slower. Locally it's roughly 375 ns more per call. Not a big deal next to the file system calls, but it's paid by every caller, including the ones that use the defaults.

I think it can be avoided without changing the behavior at all:

- Only validate values passed by the caller. The defaults (`template` and an empty suffix) never contain a directory, so `mkstemp()` with no arguments doesn't need the check.
- For exact `str` and `bytes`, check for the separator characters first, and only call `os.path.dirname()` when one is present. On POSIX that check is exact. On Windows, any value with `\`, `/` or `:` still goes through `dirna

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/c63aec69bd59c55314c06c23f4c22c03de76fe45/Python/pystate.c#L1783-L1818

If one of those finalizers creates a new `asyncio.Task`, `register_task()` inserts it into `_PyThreadState_GET()`'s own task list:

`_PyThreadState_GET()` still returns the thread calling `PyThreadState_Clear()` on itself, now past the merge point. The Task is otherwise ordinary: nothing is wrong with it, and the event loop that owns it runs it to completion normally, on another thread. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/c63aec69bd59c55314c06c23f4c22c03de76fe45/Modules/_asynciomodule.c#L2211-L2220

### Bug Description

This is the **tracking issue** for the `no_link_attr_used` future-compatibility warning and other related errors. The goal of this page is to describe why this change was made and how you can fix code that is affected by it. It also provides a place to ask questions or register a complaint if you feel the change should not be made. For more information on the policy around future-compatibility warnings, see our [breaking change policy guidelines][guidelines].

[guidelines]: https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/bug-fix-procedure.html

### What is the warning for?

Usage of the `#[no_link]` attribute.

### Why was this change made?

This is a pre-1.0 attribute that accidentally got stabilized. It was only meant for compiler plugins which we no longer support, not for regular crates. It is rather fragile and can easily lead to linker errors depending on where rustc decides to codegen functions and statics, which varies between rustc versions. It might also be unsound if a crate for example expects a global constructor it defined to run. Using it doesn't have an effect on the size of the produced binaries except when it defines a #[used] static given that we remove all unused functions and statics at link time already.

### Example

```rust
#[no_link]
extern crate foo;
```

### Recommendations

Remove the `#[no_link]` attribute.

### When will this warning become a hard error?

Possibly in a couple of releases given that a crater run showed barely any usage.

utf-8-sig: UnicodeDecodeError offsets do not count the BOM

### Bug report

When the input starts with a BOM, the utf-8-sig codec reports `UnicodeDecodeError` offsets relative to the input without the BOM, i.e. `error.start` is off-by-3:

```python
data = b"\xef\xbb\xbf\xff"  # Invalid byte at position 3
try:
    data.decode("utf-8-sig")
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    print(e)  # 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 0: invalid start byte
```

The input is being sliced in `utf_8_sig.py` to remove the BOM, but raised exceptions are not modified to correct the offsets and object attributes. This occurs in a few places, e.g. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/5a22a62b96a68c2dd31784c5e3427ad7b365388a/Lib/encodings/utf_8_sig.py#L18-L24

The utf-16 and utf-32 codecs also remove the BOM, but it is included in the offsets and object attributes in their errors, so this looks like an oversight.

del StopIteration.value stores NULL in C field, crashing generators (SIGSEGV)

### Crash report

`del e.value` on a `StopIteration` instance stores NULL into
`PyStopIterationObject.value`. The getter substitutes `Py_None` so it
looks fine at Python level, but two C consumers dereference it unconditionally.

**Consumer 1** — `genobject.c:818`, `gen_send_ex2`:
```c
value = Py_NewRef(((PyStopIterationObject *)exc)->value);  // Py_NewRef(NULL) → SIGSEGV
```

Reproducer:
```python
def gen():
    yield 1
g = gen()
next(g)
e = StopIteration(99)
del e.value
g.send(None)  # Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

**Consumer 2** — `bytecodes.c:1971`, `CLEANUP_THROW`:
```c
value = PyStackRef_FromPyObjectNew(...)  // assert(obj != NULL) → SIGABRT/SIGSEGV
```

Reproducer:
```python
class It:
    def __iter__(self): return self
    def __next__(self): return 1
    def throw(self, typ, val=None, tb=None):
        e = StopIteration(99)
        del e.value
        raise e
def outer():
    yield from It()
g = outer()
next(g)
g.throw(ValueError)  # Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

Both confirmed on main at `5a22a62b96a`.

**Root cause** — `exceptions.c:721` declares `value` as `_Py_T_OBJECT` with
`flags=0`, which permits `del`. Fix: use `_Py_T_OBJECT_EX` or add `Py_READONLY`,
or add NULL guards in both consumers.

Found while auditing CPython with a static-analysis toolkit flagging `Py_NewRef`/`Py_XNewRef` mismatches.

`func_get_annotation_dict` missing critical section after gh-128714

### Bug report

gh-128714 added `@critical_section` to the `__annotations__` setter and deleter, but the getter (`function___annotations___get_impl`) and its helper `func_get_annotation_dict` were not protected.

```c
// NO @critical_section on the getter
static PyObject *
function___annotations___get_impl(PyFunctionObject *self)
{
    ...
    d = func_get_annotation_dict(self);  // reads + Py_XSETREF without lock
}

// line ~976 — setter has @critical_section, getter does not
```

`func_get_annotation_dict` (line 539) does an unprotected read of `op->func_annotations` and a `Py_XSETREF` into it at line 557. A concurrent setter holds a critical section; the getter does not. This is a read-write race.

Inline the per-item equality check in `list.__contains__/index/count/remove`

### Feature or enhancement

`list.__contains__()`, `index()`, `count()`, `remove()`, and element comparisons in `list.__eq__()` use `PyObject_RichCompareBool()` for each element.

During a scan, the search value is fixed. Since we already know its type and its value, when an element has the same exact built-in type (int, float, or str), its comparison implementation is already known. Going through generic rich-comparison dispatch adds unnecessary type-dispatch and slot-handling overhead.

Add a fast path for these exact-type pairs, fall back to `PyObject_RichCompareBool()` for other cases.

Use-after-free in PyObject_CallFinalizer when __del__ changes __class__

### Bug description

`PyObject_CallFinalizer()` keeps a borrowed pointer to the object's original type across `tp_finalize(self)`. A Python `__del__` method can change `self.__class__`; cyclic GC can then free the original heap type before `PyObject_CallFinalizer()` reads `tp->tp_flags` again, causing a heap use-after-free.

This reproduces on current `main` in a release-mode AddressSanitizer build. The same PoC also reproduces without the explicit `gc.collect()` call when ordinary allocations trigger collection.

```python
import gc

class Survivor:
    pass

def make():
    class Temporal:
        def __del__(self):
            self.__class__ = Survivor
            gc.collect()
    return Temporal()

victim = make()
del victim
```

The relevant sequence is:

```c
PyTypeObject *tp = Py_TYPE(self);
tp->tp_finalize(self);       // __del__ changes self.__class__; GC frees tp
if (_PyType_IS_GC(tp)) {     // reads the freed type
    _PyGC_SET_FINALIZED(self);
}
```

    CFLAGS='-O1 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer'

$ ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 ./python.exe poc.py

tkinter and IDLE tests depend on buggy Tk behavior for unmapped text widgets

Several tests fail with Tcl/Tk 9.0.5 and 9.1.1:

* `test_tkinter.test_text.TextTest.test_count`
* `idle_test.test_codecontext.CodeContextTest.test_toggle_code_context_event`, `test_update_code_context` and `test_jumptoline`
* `idle_test.test_sidebar.LineNumbersTest.test_scroll`

A text widget which has not been mapped yet has size 1x1, and Tk used to lay out its content in that area, putting every character on its own display line. This was fixed in [784c08a4c9](https://core.tcl-lang.org/tk/info/784c08a4c9): such a widget is now laid out at its requested size. The tests above depended on the old buggy behavior.

`test_count` expects a non-zero number of vertical pixels between the indices `1.3` and `1.5`, but they are on the same display line, for which `-ypixels` returns zero. The `codecontext` tests scroll the text widget, but the code sample is shorter than the now visible height. `test_scroll` needs the real geometry of mapped widgets; it fails with Tk 8.6 too when run alone.

The fix is on `core-9-0-branch` after the 9.0.4 release and on trunk after 9.1.0, so this will affect all branches once Tk 9.0.5 and 9.1.1 are released.

Cannot implement public trait with private type arg on public type in std due to stability attr lints

Encountered in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/162849#issuecomment-6099889602

You cannot write an impl of this form in std:
```rust
struct MyPtr<T: ?Sized>(NonNull<T>);

// #[unstable(feature = "box_internals", issue = "none")]
impl<T: ?Sized> From<MyPtr<T>> for NonNull<T> {
    fn from(value: MyPtr<T>) -> Self {
        self.0
    }
}
```

Without the attribute, you get an error:
```sh
error: implementation has missing stability attribute
   --> ...
    |
    | impl<T: ?Sized> From<BoxRaw<T>> for NonNull<T> {
    | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```
With the attribute, you get a deny-by-default lint:
```sh
error: an `#[unstable]` annotation here has no effect
   --> ...
    |
    | #[unstable(feature = "box_internals", issue = "none")]
    | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    |
    = note: see issue #55436 <https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/55436> for more information
    = note: `#[deny(ineffective_unstable_trait_impl)]` on by default
```

So in general, the only option is to allow the lint.

Run the Python test suite in parallel by default

Currently, `python -m test` runs tests sequentially in a single process by default. It's slow and unsafe: if a test does crash, the whole test suite is interrupted, we don't exit cleanly, and resources may not be released properly (a temporary directory can be left behind).

I propose to run the Python test suite in parallel by default: choose the number of worker processes using `os.process_cpu_count()`. In short, make `-j0` option the default. Running tests in parallel makes the task way faster (especially on machines with 8 CPUs or more). When using `-j0`, the test suite main process just watchs worker processes and is way likely to crash. When a worker process does crash, its working directory is removed cleanly. Also, when tests are interrupted by CTRL+C, the main process makes sure that all worker processes are stopped or killed (including child processes).

Instead, you will have to use `--single-process` explicitly to opt-in for Python 3.15 behavior: run tests sequentially in a single process.

Generator expression over extension type attribute fails with `TypeError: 'functools.partial'` object is not iterable in 3.15

### Bug report

In Python 3.15, generator expressions evaluating an attribute on an extension type with custom `tp_getattro` pass a `functools.partial` object to the generator rather than the attribute itself, raising:
```
TypeError: 'functools.partial' object is not iterable
```

```python
from PySide6.QtCore import Qt
# Python 3.15: TypeError: 'functools.partial' object is not iterable
# Python <= 3.14: Works
gen = (k for k in Qt.Key)
# Direct iteration always works:
[k for k in Qt.Key]
```

#### Possible cause: 
Generator expression setup emits `LOAD_ATTR` followed directly by `CALL 0` to pass the iterable to the generator closure.
This adjacency causes extension types implementing custom `tp_getattro` (reproduced with PySide6/Shiboken `abi3`) to treat the access as a call target, passing `functools.partial` to `GET_ITER`.
Inserting a `NOP` between `LOAD_ATTR` and `CALL 0` avoids the issue.

```py
import dis
from PySide6.QtCore import Qt
code = compile('(k for k in Qt.Key)', '', 'eval')
bc = bytearray(code.co_code)
idx = bc.index(dis.opmap['CALL'])
bc.insert(idx, 0)
bc.insert(idx, dis.opmap['NOP'])
g = eval(code.replace(co_code=bytes(bc)))
print(next(g))
```


### CPython versions tested on:

3.15

### Operating systems tested on:

Windows 11 x64

This has also been reported to the PySide6 bug tracker https://qt-project.atlassian.net/browse/PYSIDE-3481

_Py_Mangle reads out of bounds for one-char identifiers

### Bug description

`_Py_Mangle()` in `Python/symtable.c` calls `PyUnicode_READ_CHAR(ident, 1)` without first checking that `ident` has at least two characters. If `ident` is a one-character string (e.g. `"_"`), this reads one code point past the end of the unicode buffer.

The read is silent in release builds because a 1-char ASCII unicode object has enough padding for the null terminator, so ASAN does not trip. But it is still UB per the `PyUnicode_READ_CHAR` contract.

### Reproducer

```python
class C:
    _
```

### Call path
_Py_Mangle entry check:

```c
if (privateobj == NULL || !PyUnicode_Check(privateobj) ||
    PyUnicode_READ_CHAR(ident, 0) != '_' ||
    PyUnicode_READ_CHAR(ident, 1) != '_') {
    return Py_NewRef(ident);
}
```

For ident == "_", READ_CHAR(ident, 0) != '_' is false, so READ_CHAR(ident, 1) is evaluated — out of bounds.

### Comparison
_Py_IsPrivateName() in the same file does guard with nlen < 3 before indexing. The guard is missing from _Py_Mangle().

### Suggested fix
Add PyUnicode_GET_LENGTH(ident) < 2 || to the condition.

### Documentation discrepancy

The description of `csv.Sniffer.has_header()` says that a majority of columns plus rows determines the result and that a differing string length is evidence for a header. At main revision `77f7b96c2c77ac6d83155fe2659513ee6bcd5623`, the implementation instead discards columns whose sampled types/lengths are inconsistent, then adds one positive or negative vote per remaining column. A tie returns `False`.

Sources: [documentation](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/77f7b96c2c77ac6d83155fe2659513ee6bcd5623/Doc/library/csv.rst), [implementation](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/77f7b96c2c77ac6d83155fe2659513ee6bcd5623/Lib/csv.py).

### Reproduction isolating header voting

```python
import csv

class FixedComma(csv.Sniffer):
    def sniff(self, sample, delimiters=None):
        return csv.excel

s = FixedComma()
assert s.has_header("filename,path\nc.txt,/tmp/c.txt\npython.txt,/tmp/python.txt\n") is False
assert s.has_header("name,cc\n1,aa\n2,bb\n") is False
assert s.has_header("name,kind\n1,a\n2,bbbb\n") is True
```

The first sample excludes both columns due to varying lengths. The second has one positive and one negative vote. The third excludes the second column and retains a positive numeric-column vote. These are not requests to change the heuristic: the proposed fix is documentation-only and retains its false-positive/false-negative warning.

import os

except OSError as exc:

os._exit(0)
'''

`marshal.dumps()` raises `TypeError` for a set containing several complex NaNs

### Bug report

`marshal` writes the elements of a set in the order of a sort of
`(marshalled bytes, value)` pairs.  When two elements have the same
marshalled bytes, the sort compares the values.  Complex numbers are not
orderable, so this fails:

```python
>>> import marshal
>>> marshal.dumps(frozenset({complex('nan'), complex('nan')}))
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'complex' and 'complex'
```

Two distinct elements only have the same bytes when they are NaNs that are
different objects (or containers of such NaNs).

The compiler can produce such a constant by folding, so the code object
cannot be marshalled and no `.pyc` can be written for the module:

```python
>>> code = compile("x in {(1e999-1e999)*1j, (1e999-1e999)*2j}", "m.py", "exec")
>>> code.co_consts
(inf, frozenset({(nan+nanj), (nan+nanj)}))
>>> marshal.dumps(code)
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'complex' and 'complex'
```

A related problem in the same code: float NaNs do compare, but neither way,
so elements with equal bytes stay in set iteration order, which depends on
their addresses.  If one of them is also referenced elsewhere in the dump,
the output differs for the same value:

```python
import marshal
nans = [float('nan') for _ in range(3)]
# A list of a NaN and a set of three NaNs, one of which is that NaN.
print(len({marshal.dumps([n, set(nans)]) for n in nans}))   # 3, expected 1
```

`marshal.dumps()` crashes when a set is modified while it is being marshalled

### Crash report

To sort the elements of a set, `w_complex_object()` reads the size of the
set, allocates a list of that size, then marshals each element on its own
in a loop.  Marshalling an element can run Python code (an element's
`__buffer__`, an audit hook), and that code can change the set.  If the set
grows, the loop writes past the end of the list.  If it shrinks, the list
is left with NULL items and is then sorted.

```python
import marshal, sys

class Item:
    def __hash__(self):
        return 0
    def __buffer__(self, flags):
        if sys.argv[1] == 'grow':
            s.update(range(1000, 1400))
        else:
            s.difference_update(range(1, 60))
        return memoryview(b'abc')

s = {Item()}
s.update(range(1, 60))
marshal.dumps(s)
```

On main:

- `shrink`, release build: segmentation fault.
- `grow`, release build: no error; writes past the list allocation.
- `grow`, debug build:
  `PyList_SET_ITEM: Assertion 'index < list->allocated' failed.`

On the free-threaded build another thread changing the set between the size
read and the critical section has the same effect.

### Proposed fix

Stop the loop at the size that was read, and raise
`RuntimeError("set changed size during iteration")` if the number of
elements seen differs from it, as iterating a set does.

Speed up bytes.join() when all items are exact bytes

### Feature or enhancement

`bytes.join()` and `bytearray.join()` fill a `Py_buffer` and take a reference for every item, even when all items are exact `bytes`. With more than 10 items, that also means allocating the array of `Py_buffer`s. On the free-threaded build the increfs are atomic when the items are shared between threads, and since gh-158803 they run while the list's lock is held.

When every item is exact `bytes` and the result is below the 1 MiB threshold at which `join()` releases the GIL, nothing can run Python code or suspend the critical section. So the items can be copied straight from the sequence, without a `Py_buffer` or a reference for each one. Other inputs keep the current path.

Release builds, `b",".join(seq)` with distinct 8-byte items:

| | FT main | FT patched | default main | default patched |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| list of 10 | 170 ns | 92 ns | 138 ns | 79 ns |
| list of 1000 | 11.0 µs | 4.3 µs | 10.0 µs | 4.0 µs |
| 8 threads joining one shared list of 100 | 0.60 s | 0.18 s | | |

Lists with non-bytes items take the general path, which can be a bit slower depending on the compiler's inlining (see the discussion in #159096).

Tachyon: use bounded columnar blocks for binary profiles

Tachyon currently stores samples in one compressed stream. The reader decompresses the whole sample section before replay, so long captures need a large allocation.

I propose small blocks with separate columns for thread and interpreter IDs, timestamps, flags, stack changes, and frame indices. Each block stores each thread/interpreter pair once. Samples refer to that pair with a small index. Timestamps store the difference from the expected sample time, without loss of precision. Stacks reuse common frames or refer to a previous stack in the same block.

Each column can use zstd, a single repeated value, or raw bytes, whichever is smaller. Similar values sit together, which can help compression. The reader processes one block at a time, so its sample buffer no longer grows with capture length. Shared string and frame tables still need memory.

The aim is smaller files and cheaper replay. We need to preserve the current format’s efficiency for repeated stacks. This needs a new format version, with the same public collector and replay APIs. Live output remains separate work in #145464.

Some C code in the interpreter and standard library still performs reference-counting operations on objects already known to be `Py_None`.

IDNA incremental encoder reports wrong error offset when a non-ASCII label precedes the invalid one

The error offset reported by `encodings.idna.IncrementalEncoder` is
computed from the str length of preceding labels, but the encoder
writes the punycode-encoded bytes. For non-ASCII labels these differ,
so the reported offset is too small.

Reproducer:

    import codecs
    enc = codecs.getincrementalencoder("idna")()
    enc.encode("é")              # held in the buffer
    enc.encode("." + "a"*64, True)

This raises UnicodeEncodeError with start=2, end=66. The correct
offset is start=8, end=72, since "é" encodes to b"xn--9ca" (7 bytes)
plus the b"." separator (1 byte).

The bug is in Lib/encodings/idna.py, IncrementalEncoder._buffer_encode:

    size += len(label)

`label` is a str, but `result.extend(ToASCII(label))` appends the
punycode-encoded bytes. `size` should track the bytes written, so it
should be `size += len(encoded)` (with `ToASCII` called once).

I'm happy to open a PR with a fix and a test.

### Crash report

In the free-threaded build, `dict()` and `dict.update()` can crash when an item of the iterable is a list that another thread mutates. `merge_from_seq2_lock_held()` in `Objects/dictobject.c` checks that the pair has two items, then reads both with `PySequence_Fast_GET_ITEM()`, which returns borrowed references, without holding the list's lock. def writer():
    for _ in range(10000):
        pair.clear()
        pair.extend((object(), object()))
    done.set()

    while not done.is_set():
        try:
            dict([pair])
        except ValueError:
            pass

threads = [threading.Thread(target=writer)]
threads += [threading.Thread(target=reader) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:

```

`re`: no ASCII fast path for `\w` in Unicode mode, unlike `\s`

### Feature or enhancement

Use the existing ASCII table to speed up word matching for ASCII characters, while keeping Unicode by default.

For example:

```python
>>> import re
>>> re.findall(r"\w+", "hello café 123")
['hello', 'café', '123']
```

Most characters in this example are ASCII, but the `re` still uses Unicode classification for each character that `\w` examines.

## Idea

The idea is for chars less than 128, use `SRE_IS_WORD()`. For the rest, keep the existing Unicode predicate:

```c
#define SRE_UNI_IS_WORD(ch)\
    ((ch) < 128 ? SRE_IS_WORD(ch) : (SRE_UNI_IS_ALNUM(ch) || (ch) == '_'))
```

The same predicate is used by `\W`, `\b` and `\B` so it'd speed them up, too.

We're doing it for `\s`:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/9028df36bb9e2942b19164f6708f9cf8a55c5ce9/Include/cpython/unicodeobject.h#L753-L758

Stack frame regression in 1.99 (LLVM 23): MemCpyOpt merges allocas and drops the lifetime markers of the merge target

### Summary

Upgrading from Rust 1.98.1 (LLVM 22.1.8) to 1.99.0 (LLVM 23.1.1) increases the stack frames of some functions that copy values out of an out-of-line call result inside a branch. `Clone` impls on nested `Option`s hit this pattern, whether derived or written by hand. In the reduced example below the frame grows by 36%. In our real code, the derived `Clone` of a recursive SQL AST type grew by 71% (2504 B to 4328 B), and a SQL planner that recurses through this `clone` now overflows a 2 MiB thread stack at 338 nesting levels instead of 564. The process aborts with `has overflowed its stack`.

The growth comes from LLVM 23's MemCpyOpt pass. When a `memcpy` copies from an offset inside a larger alloca into smaller allocas, LLVM 23 replaces the smaller allocas with pointers into the larger one and deletes the larger alloca's `llvm.lifetime.start`/`llvm.lifetime.end` markers. An alloca without markers is live for the whole function, so StackColoring can no longer share its slot with temporaries of other branches. LLVM 22's MemCpyOpt does not perform this replacement on the same input. This looks like the same mechanism as #161568, which this issue pins to a stable-to-stable regression.

Docs: `:deco:` references with `~` render as `@~module.name`

### Documentation

Decorator cross-references written with the tilde short form, e.g. ``:deco:`~typing.dataclass_transform` ``, render literally as **`@~typing.dataclass_transform`** instead of `@dataclass_transform`. The link target is correct; only the title is wrong.

See e.g. [What's New In Python 3.11 – PEP 681](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.11.html#pep-681-data-class-transforms).

## Cause

The `deco` role is Sphinx's own (`_PyDecoXRefRole`). In Sphinx 8.2.3, it prepends `@` in `update_title_and_target()`, which runs *before* `PyXRefRole.process_link()`. `process_link()` then checks `title[0:1] == '~'`, sees `@`, and leaves the tilde and module prefix in place. Sphinx 9.x prepends the `@` in `process_link()` after the tilde handling, so it renders correctly.

These references were introduced in gh-139598 (gh-105812). That landed while `Doc/requirements.txt` was pinned to `sphinx<9.0.0` (gh-143284, to work around Chinese search in Sphinx 9), so the docs build hits the Sphinx 8 bug.

## Possible fixes

1. Unpin and go back to Sphinx 9 once the gh-143284 search issue is resolved. That fixes every instance with no `.rst` changes.
2. Rewrite each reference with an explicit title, e.g. ``:deco:`dataclass_transform <typing.dataclass_transform>` ``, or drop the `~` (``:deco:`typing.dataclass_transform` ``).

Cache an exact byte offset for specialized global and module loads

`LOAD_GLOBAL_MODULE`, `LOAD_GLOBAL_BUILTIN`, and `LOAD_ATTR_MODULE` all currently cache an index into a dictionary's values. This is much faster than a normal lookup, but still requires calculating the exact internal layout of the keys each time in order to turn that index into an actual pointer to the value.

```c
PyObject **value = (char *)keys + 32 + (1 << keys->dk_log2_index_bytes) + 16 * cache + 8;
```

Instead, we can just cache a byte offset from `ma_keys`, calculated at specialization time:

```c
PyObject **value = (char *)keys + cache;
```

This is about a 1% win on pyperformance. It doesn't benefit the JIT when cached values are promoted to constants, but the JIT does in benefit the case where a dictionary has been modified "too many" times and the lookup doesn't get constified.

I have an implementation and will open a PR soon.

tarfile produces invalid pax archives when a gname is exactly 32 bytes long

### Bug report

This is a pretty minor bug, but it's also technically a form of pax non-conformance. 

See https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/22510 for context.

## Summary

TL;DR: the original tar format allocates a fixed 32 byte block for the `gname` field. pax says that this field should always be NUL terminated, meaning that any group name above 31 bytes in length should be encoded via a `gname` extension instead:

Ref: [pax spec](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/utilities/pax.html#:~:text=The%20fields%20magic,or%20NUL%20characters.)

However, what tarfile does is use _all_ of the 32 bytes for content, with no NUL terminator. Many tar parsers recover from this, since the pax spec confusingly _does_ allow this kind of non-termination in _other_ fields (like `name`, `linkname`, and `prefix`). However, it's always incorrect for `gname` as well as `magic` and `uname`.

The fix here is behavior preserving: pax also allowing supplying the `gname` as an arbitrary-length pax extension, and pax emitters should emit that extension when a `gname` is longer than 31 bytes. pax extensions are always given precedence over their header counterparts, so this is fully compatible.

(A conforming pax emitter can also choose to emit pax extensions unconditionally, even when the values _would_ fit in the header.)

Rust 1.98.0 (and later).
